title: Student-led protests in Albania turn violent as thousands call for prime minister to resign
summary: Clashes broke out Saturday between police and protesters in the Albanian capital, Tirana, as thousands of people called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, the latest in a long series of…

image.caption: A person wearing a mask holds a lit flare by the Skanderbeg Monument during an anti-government protest on Albania's Independence Day in Tirana, the capital, on Saturday. (Florion Goga/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Clashes broke out Saturday between police and protesters in the Albanian capital, Tirana, as thousands of people called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, the latest in a long series of anti-government protests.
Protest is the latest in a series of demonstrations against government corruption
The protest began peacefully, but small groups of masked demonstrators broke away and began smashing the windows of government buildings along the march route.

Police used tear gas and water cannons to push back protesters throwing rocks and Molotov cocktails and using wooden sticks to try to smash street cameras and windows on government buildings. Clouds of tear gas billowed through the area as protesters spread out across several streets.
An officer fires a crowd-control weapon, as police face off against demonstrators during an anti-government protest in Tirana on Saturday. (Florion Goga/Reuters)

Albanians travelled to Tirana from across the country and abroad for the rally, which coincided with Albania's Independent Day, which is normally marked by celebrations and a public holiday. Police were deployed along the main roads leading in and out of the capital, conducting vehicle checks.
"I came here specifically for the protest," said Arian Lleshi, a 33-year-old who travelled from the United Kingdom.

"Why? Because we have been suffering for far too long. We have spread ourselves across Europe and around the world, and it is almost as if we are citizens without a state. We are like stateless citizens."
Police detain a protester during Saturday's student-led demonstrations in Albania's capital. (Hameraldi Agolli/The Associated Press)

The political parties that have been around in Albania since the fall of communism in the 1990s "no longer represent anyone," Lleshi said. "They need to make way for a new generation of intellectuals and people who have a greater stake in the country’s future."
Saturday’s protest was part of a series of demonstrations that began in late May.

items: How Ivanka Trump helped spark Albania's 'Flamingo Revolution'

blocks.text: They were initially sparked by opposition to a major luxury tourism development on Albania's southern coast that is linked to an investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
The protests became known as the "Flamingo Revolution" and have since been followed by more demonstrations.
A gasoline bomb bursts into flames next to police officers in riot gear in Tirana. (Florion Goga/Reuters)
Fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, lack of jobs and poor education standards, more recent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since mid-October and spread to other cities.
They have often turned violent, with protesters setting fire to government buildings and banks, smashing shop windows and pulling up paving stones to throw at police.

items: Protests in Albania over planned luxury resort linked to Trump's son-in-law

blocks.text: The demonstrators' demands have since broadened to include calls for Rama's resignation. The prime minister has governed Albania since 2013. On Saturday, protesters chanted "Resignation!" as they gathered in Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square.
"Enough is enough; the corruption, the poverty, the immigration," said Eralda Baze, 45, an engineer who joined Saturday's rally.
Demonstrators attempt to flee as police deploy water cannons against them while clamping down on anti-government protests in Albania's capital. (Florion Goga/Reuters)
"We have come out to demand our rights. We have had enough. Life has become very difficult. We are calling for a change to the entire system," student Juna Vasili said.

Suzana Gjeta, a retiree, said she was demonstrating both on behalf of young people and those like herself "who are living on just 120 euros a month.... We hope this system will go, that Edi Rama will go and that this corruption will end."

blocks.text: Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years, and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Albania is leading a posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the European Union and is aiming for entry by 2030.
Demonstrators face off against police in Tirana on Saturday. (Florion Goga/Reuters)
